title: How are you finding players and reaching creators when your game uses AI assets?
author: thvaz
selftext:
I'm a solo developer and released the Steam demo for Submundus today. It's a dungeon crawler with deckbuilding and survival mechanics. I use AI in development, including assets, and disclose it on the Steam page.

My approach so far has been to be open about it without making AI the game's selling point. I talk about the game itself, answer honestly if asked, and leave negative comments about AI use alone. I'm happy to discuss problems with the game, but I don't want to spend launch day arguing about whether AI should exist.

Creator outreach was also discouraging with my previous game: the only replies I got were from scammers. I'd like to hear from people who've had better experiences.

Do you know any YouTubers or streamers who are willing to cover games with disclosed AI use? They don't need to specialize in AI games or support AI publicly, just be interested in playing something in their genre regardless of how some assets were made. Deckbuilders, roguelites and turn-based dungeon crawlers would be particularly relevant.

If you've released a game using AI, what actually helped you reach players? Specific channels, communities, or examples of coverage would be useful, even if the results were small.

I'm keeping the disclosure either way. I'm trying to figure out where outreach is worth the effort.

If it's not good enough to spend your own hard earned money on it, why expect anyone to want to play it?  Do you believe in your project?  If you want to get rich off slop it's probably not going to happen.  If it's good, then you shouldn't have a problem with spending money on it.

replies.author: thvaz

replies.author: Agitated_Quail_1430
replies.body:
Become your own biggest fan then. Make your own content and upload it to every platform you can find. Maybe start a twitch channel and play the game while talking to chat.  

There is unfortunately a lot of anti-AI sentiment. I would imagine it will take awhile for most people to come around.  But I think these big channels get people sending them games all day every day.  They cover the ones they think will get the most views and the ones they get paid for.

replies.author: waypostmaster

comments.author: WiredBrew
comments.body:
In your case, I would imagine normally?

IDK about your last game. But this game doesn't read as "AI Slop" on the surface, which is what most people care about imo. There will be some people who will be universally anti-ai, but I don't think that's the majority of people. And people will be generally more forgiving to small/solo indie projects. 

That said your game and Steam page doesn't look like something outside the "90% of games on Steam" Not as a dig against you or your project, but you know. Just saying that some of the disinterest you might encounter is less of "this is an AI game" and more of "this is just another indie game".

comments.author: Dhaupin
comments.body:
If the game is good enough, most players won't care. What you're seeing is a vocal "anti-ai" minority, attenlting to seed or "brigade" the internet with their stance.

Let them be all hot and bothered about it. It may be a blessing in disguise - many of these types of folks would nitpick some other stuff, or find things to complain about instead, or just be generally douschy with ai conspiracies about how they still don't believe this or that about some asset/mechanic being actually crafted by you.

It's all just a waste of time. Let them boycott or whatever, who cares. Theyre not gonna change the hearts and minds of most casual players, and certainly not the devs.

To compare this regarded behavior to something in the past: when tractors came out, there were vocally anti-tractor farmers. Like they wanted to work the land by hand or with horses. Look where that got them (amish, lol). The rest of the world moved on.

replies.author: drallcom3
replies.body:
> What you're seeing is a vocal "anti-ai" minority, attempting to seed or "brigade" the internet with their stance.

It's more like you need a critical mass of players to drown out the anti-AI crusader reviews.

replies.author: Dhaupin
replies.body: The critical mass of farmers succeeded in drowning out the Amish whom were against tractors. Gaming, or any other Ai backed development, will have the same results, guaranteed.

replies.body: Luckily all the big companies who now all have some form of AI disclaimer will tire out the crusaders. We should learn from them though how to best frame and phrase AI usage. No need to make it easy for them and real players will judge the game as a game anyway.

comments.author: kopko222
comments.body: Tried your demo just now, honestly its a good foundation but nothing special about it. I like the graphics style, but the combat is boring. I dont understand the whole discard cards to perform action, all the rooms I just bluntly clicked on any cards just to move further and progress, it was repetitive in the 2nd room already. The market is overcrowded with games right now, you need polished product to even catch someones attention

replies.author: thvaz
replies.body:
Thanks for trying it and being specific. When you say you clicked any card to progress, do you mean choosing cards to discard for room actions? Was it unclear how that worked, or did you understand it but feel that the choice didn't matter?

The idea is that exploration and combat share the same deck, and reshuffling advances time. Discarding cards for exploration actions makes those actions take time without putting exploration-only cards into your combat hand. But that connection may not be coming across in the opening rooms.

Your feedback helps me identify what needs work in the tutorial. Glad you liked the graphics, too.

replies.author: kopko222
replies.body: It felt like it didn't really matter, and yes I didnt caught the connection with exploration / combat. I think it might be worth to add tooltips as a new player starts a new game instead of tutorial only. Simple two sentences could explain it very well during the early game. One more thing about the combat I think the main issue with it for me was lack of the impact. It didnt have that good feedback when landing a hit that would make me feel like I did something. The targeting also need some autolocking radius, mainly for the room where was the flying bug and it was more far more away on the screen.

replies.author: thvaz

comments.author: TheFrandroid
comments.body:
We still have writers, artists and a designed world, and the AI is there to tailor the experience around the player. For creators, the hook of You vs Zombies is basically “make yourself, make something ridiculous, see what the game turns it into”. That’s been much easier to talk about than leading with the tech itself.

So I’d say we’re selling the player experience first, AI second.

comments.author: Acceptable-Wing-3789
comments.body:
I work in creator marketing so I can help you with the outreach. 

The key of a successful creator campaign is Quality +  Offering X Quantity  
  
Quality comes from prospecting, you have to make sure its the right creator for your product and they are in the right niche  
  
Offering is whats there for them. Regardless you are paying via commission or upfront payment. You should let them know clearly. Also I would recommend additional offering for example free access to your game. 

Lastly, creator marketing needs quantity. Content alignment, content calendar, responsiveness are all the factors for conversion. So do reach out to a lot of creators and dont take any personally.
